subject: Accounting
title: Asset Accounts
description: A quick win: understand Asset Accounts.

hook.text: Cash, equipment, inventory, buildings—asset accounts track everything a company owns.

buildup.text: Each type of asset gets its own account: one for cash, one for receivables, one for equipment.

discovery.text: Buy a truck with cash and the cash account drops while the vehicle account rises.

twist.text: Some assets lose value over time—depreciation slowly writes down their worth each year.

climax.text: Accurate asset accounts let managers know exactly what resources they have to work with.

punchline.text: You can't manage what you don't track.

quiz.question: What happens when a business buys equipment with cash?

details.summary: Asset accounts track everything a company owns or controls that has economic value—from cash and inventory to buildings and patents. This topic covers how assets are classified, recorded, and reported on the balance sheet.
details.whyItMatters: Assets represent the resources a company uses to generate revenue. Understanding asset accounts is fundamental to reading balance sheets and assessing a company's financial health.
takeaways: Assets are classified as current (convertible to cash within one year) or non-current (long-term)
Assets are initially recorded at cost and may be adjusted for depreciation, amortization, or impairment
Common asset accounts include cash, accounts receivable, inventory, equipment, and intangible assets

faq.question: What is the difference between current and non-current assets?
faq.answer: Current assets can be converted to cash or consumed within one year (cash, inventory, accounts receivable). Non-current assets provide value over multiple years (buildings, equipment, patents). This classification helps stakeholders assess the company's short-term liquidity.

faq.question: Why are assets recorded at cost instead of market value?
faq.answer: The cost principle records assets at their purchase price because it's objective and verifiable. Market values fluctuate and involve estimates. However, certain assets like investments may be adjusted to fair value, and impairment rules require write-downs when value declines permanently.
